A3 REPORT: ELECTRICAL ARC FLASH INCIDENT
Site: SMO1
Date of Incident: January 20, 2025, 11:45 AM
Report Date: January 27, 2026
________________________________________
BACKGROUND
On January 20, 2025, at approximately 11:45 AM, an electrical arc flash incident occurred in the MDF cage at SMO1 involving an Eaton contractor performing battery removal work on an SDEN unit. This work was initiated following a network action to remove batteries in response to a previous fire incident at another site.
Injuries Sustained:
•	Contractor: Burn injuries to hand (index finger)
•	IT Engineer (monitoring): Hearing damage
________________________________________
PROBLEM STATEMENT
During battery removal, the contractor cut into a live electrical wire still being fed from the battery, resulting in an arc flash event causing injuries to two individuals.
________________________________________
CURRENT STATE ANALYSIS
Incident Sequence
1.	Contractor was removing internal lineup batteries from UPS
2.	Contractor disconnected top string/wire but failed to disconnect remaining wires in lineup
3.	Contractor cut live wiring instead of cutting tie wraps and taping unplugged wires
4.	Arc flash event occurred, causing injuries
Root Cause
Primary: Failure to follow standard work procedures for live electrical work. The contractor failed to disconnect electrical lines prior to cutting them—a fundamental safety requirement.
Contributing Factors
Procedural Failures:
•	Project not executed according to Amazon CRM standards
•	Electrical work managed by IT instead of RME due to emergent situation
•	Standard safety protocols bypassed
Avetta Compliance Deficiencies:
•	Project site POC lacked full knowledge of Avetta process
•	Work site safety project started but not completed
•	Training certifications not uploaded to project
•	JSA attached but loaded into wrong section of Avetta page
•	JSA insufficient regarding scope of work, hazard identification, and PPE requirements
•	Company was Avetta compliant, but individual employee was not
•	Employee missin

column48: On March 29th, 2023 at approximately 08:45AM, AA was working in the Pick process path in VNA 106/107 and at Bin C180 when AA had a Pit Incident that caused damages to the bin dividers. The AA was working on OP 205 and had cage 046 when the incident occurred. AA stated they had just finished picking a case from an elevated bin (unknown number), and was descending on their OP when their OP cage got stuck on a box that was sticking out of its bin. AA stated they moved their OP back and forth and up and down to try and get their OP unstuck from the box. The AA stated that they did not use the Help Me App because they did not want to lose their bin location, and because the managers usually take too long to answer plus they were already scared. In RME’s professional opinion, they stated that it does not take a lot of force to bend the dividers because they are made of very thin materials. There were other case sticking out of other bins in the same aisle and adjacent aisles. The VNA bin fullness is at 80% and the column fullness for 106A-M180 is 77%. The root cause of the incident is that the AA did not use the Help Me App because they stated that it removes their next location and makes them drop off their cage, they also stated that it takes too long for the managers to come and help them. Bin etiquette was a contributing factor. Actions to be taken: create a method to have bin organizers staffed on every shift so that the bins have no boxes that are overly sticking out, and create a faster method for managers to respond to Help Me Apps quicker. Figure out if the associates are easily able to move between the Help Me App and Pick without it kicking them out and making them drop their cage.

On March 9, 2026, at approximately 1:25 PM, a PIT-on-PIT collision occurred near pole K13 in the VNA area. A leader was standing at the IDRT desk located near the incident location and heard the collision occur. Upon responding to the area, two associates operating powered industrial trucks were involved.

Associate 1 (Ndiaydab) (1 year and 6 months tenure) was engaged in pallet stow operations. The associate had exited a pallet aisle traveling east and was beginning to turn into the next aisle.

At the same time, Associate 2 (yboycjah) (2 years and 2 months tenure)  trained in Case Stow at this facility on January 5, 2026 was traveling south toward the 400 aisles while operating a PIT in the case stow process path. As Associate 1 was completing the turn, Associate 2  made contact with the rear of the turret truck.

Following the incident, Associate 2 stated that he was looking down at his scanner to confirm location, while traveling and did not realize there was a PIT in front of him until the collision occurred.

Both associates were engaged in normal operational duties at the time of the incident.

Root Cause
The primary root cause of the collision was operator distraction while operating PIT equipment. Associate yboycjah diverted visual attention away from the travel path to look down at the scanner device while the PIT was still in motion, which prevented the operator from recognizing the turret truck ahead in time to stop.

A contributing factor was congestion at the aisle endcap. Multiple pallets staged near the aisle exit required the turret truck operator exiting the pallet aisle to make a wider turn, increasing the likelihood of intersecting travel paths with PIT traffic moving through the main aisle.

Both OP were red tag for RME to complete their checks after safety confirmed that no injuries had occurred. Both associates were taken to the Safety office for witness statements, and both were scheduled for drug tests, which were administered by Quest at 0137pm. At the scene of the incident, photographs were taken, and video footage was obtained. During the investigation, associate A stated that they were in line for stowing when a Clamp truck came in stow pickup Car Wash and they had to turn their OP a bit to the left and another OP ran into them, while associate B stated that they had come out of the Pit Parking and were heading straight on the far-right lane. They almost passed them when associate A turned out and never looked to check for oncoming traffic. According to the video footage, associate A was traveling on the right side of the Pit lane before turning left into associate B, who was also traveling in the same direction on the right lane. The root cause is determined to be a failure to follow traffic rules or signage. As a result of this incident, Safety has revoked both associates' Pit licenses, and they will need to be retrained.

column48: At approximately 7:50 am on 3.7.22 Safety was called over the radio to the scene of a PIT incident. The incident took place by the carwash station near racking 150. Upon arriving to the scene, Safety verified that no injuries had taken place, and both AAs were brought to the Safety office for witness statements. There was minimal damage to the OP machines involved in the incident. During the investigation, Safety found that one associate was waiting in line behind other OP machines to swoop into the carwash station. This associate, associate one, was stagnant waiting in the line when the other associate, associate two, came up from behind and hit associate one’s OP machine. The second associate attempted to stop their OP machine by depressing the deadman pedal but the machine did not stop in time and hit the fork side of the first associate’s OP machine. According to the first associate, “I was on my way to get the cage for the morning when the first person in front of me was stopped waiting for a cage or to be informed to go ahead and get one so I came to a stop and he was a good ways behind me and it sounded like he was slowing down to stop but it slid into me”. The second associate’s witness account reads as follows: “On the machine and driving to the side to pick up the cage to stow. When suddenly I got in line behind the other OPs. Traffic came to a stop and the OPs glided together. While I was slowing down and let off the deadman the OP kept going, because it had the warning light on and then it stop”. As a result of the incident, the second associate will have their OP training permissions revoked and will be retrained for OP use. The first associate was sent back to the floor and will be allowed to continue to use the OP machines because they were operating their OP correctly at the time of the incident.

column48: At approximately 4:50PM an AM walk up to Amcare to report a PIT Incident. The incident took place at the exit to aisle 182 and the entrance to aisle 181. Upon arriving to the scene, Safety verified that no injuries had taken place and both AAs were brought to the Safety Office for Witness Statement. There was little frame damage to one of the OP machines involved in the incident. During the investigation, Safety found that First Associate was exiting the aisle on aisle 182 while the other Second Associate was going into aisle 181. Frist Associate OP ran into Second Associate OP while First Associate suddenly exit the aisle 182. According to the First Associate witness account reads, “I was coming out of the aisle and I honked my horn and I did not hear a response so I pulled out and I ended bumping into my coworker”. The second Associate’s witness account reads as follows: “I was coming from one aisle driving the OP onto the next, all of a sudden after the turn the OP coming out the next aisle bumped my OP from his blindside”. As a result of the incident, the First Associate will have their OP training permissions revoked and will be retrained for OP use. The Second Associate will be sent back to the floor and will be allowed to continue to use the OP machines because they were operating their OP correctly at the time of the incident.

Both AA’s involved in the incident were brought to the Safety office. The first AA, login included above, stated that they were going to break travelling away from break room on main aisle to park their OP.  AA stated that they came to a stop at the main intersection and then proceeded through the intersection when they noticed another OP to the left of them.  The 2nd OP then kept going through the intersection and impacted the 1st OP at 90-degree angle (t-bone) in the middle of the intersection.  The first AA’s witness statement reads as follows: “I was going on break.  I was headed to 3rd picker parking lot.  I was coming to a stop when the OP driver coming from my left didn’t stop and hit the front of my OP”.  The 2nd AA, login included above, stated that they were coming down aisle between VNA and Pallet area and saw 2 OPs at intersection.  The AA then proceeded through the intersection and attempted to make a left turn to go to pit parking area for break when they did not see the other OP attempting to go straight in intersection and impacted the other OP in middle of intersection.  The 2nd AA’s witness statement reads as follows: “I was driving straight down coming to an intersection.  I looked left and right at the stop sign and saw two OPs to my right that appeared to be stopped and waiting for me to my assumption.  I honked as I turned left and hit an OP on the side that was in my blind spot”.

PIT-PIT Incident:  On 05/13/2024 at approximately 23:30 during night shift two AAs were involve in a PIT-PIT incident.  The incident occurred by pick Zone 11. An interview, witness statement and video footage were use as tools of investigation.  AA1 stated they had their OP at zone 11 and had their OP sticking out a little from zone at the time of the impact.  AA2 stated they were driving in front of zone 11 when AA1 attempted to come out of zone impacting OP.  Upon further investigation on video footage it was determined AA1 attempted to exit zone 11 impacting AA2 OP. 

ROOT CAUSE: The Root cause revealed that the primary cause of the incident was the overfilling of the zone with cages, and the improper staging of cages in a “Free from Obstruction” YELLOW and BLACK floor marking area.
 
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS: 
1.)	Close drop off zones when they are over filled with full cages
2.)	Ensure that the number of cages in each zone is controlled and limited to prevent overcrowding and to avoid cages from improperly staged in a "Free from Obstruction" designated area
3.)	Enforce accountability: Hold individuals responsible for following proper procedures and address any non-compliance promptly to address zones that are overfilled with cages

Root Cause - 5 Why's
1.	Why did the collision occur?
•	Because AA-2 was too close to the aisles while AA-1 didn't pull up far enough to see out.
2.	Why was AA-2 driving too close to the aisles?
•	Because they weren't following their trained travel paths and proper driving positions.
3.	Why wasn't AA-2 following proper travel paths?
•	Because they hadn't fully grasped the importance of maintaining safe distances from aisle entrances.
4.	Why wasn't this importance clear to AA-2?
•	Because the training may not have effectively emphasized why proper travel paths are critical for safety.
5.	Why wasn't this emphasized enough in training?
•	Because the training program might focus more on operational skills than specific safety-critical behaviors.
Root Cause: Training program needs to better emphasize critical safety behaviors, especially proper travel paths and their importance.

# Incident Report: Dock Door 31 Unloading Incident

**Date/Time:** August 16, \~10:25 PM
**Location:** Dock Door 31
**Equipment:** Powered Industrial Truck (PIT), 53’ Trailer
**Incident Type:** Unsafe Pallet Handling

Incident Summary

An associate was unloading double-stacked UPP pallets from a 53-foot trailer. After successfully removing pallets from the right side of the trailer, the associate attempted to unload a problematic double stack. Instead of moving the pallets at least 12 inches beyond the dock plate edge as required by safety protocols, the associate attempted to down stack them directly on the dock plate, creating an unstable condition.

Sequence of Events

* Associate began unloading double-stacked blue UPP pallets.
* Initial difficulty was encountered with the first stack.
* Associate successfully removed pallets from the right side.
* Associate returned to the problematic stack and moved it onto the dock plate.
* Down stacking was attempted directly on the dock plate (safety violation).
* Multiple unsuccessful attempts were made to insert PIT forks between pallets.
* Associate appeared to signal for supervisor support but continued the task.
* The bottom pallet sustained significant damage from repeated manipulation.
* Associate eventually staged the PIT away as leadership arrived.
* The damaged bottom pallet collapsed, causing the top pallet to fall and product to scatter.

Safety Violations

* Down stacking performed on the dock plate rather than beyond the required 12-inch safety zone.
* Failure to promptly escalate when encountering resistance and pallet instability.
* Continued operation despite clear signs of product damage and risk.
* Lack of situational awareness while attempting to down stack full UPP pallets.
* Failure to dismount the PIT to properly assess the situation.

Outcome

* **No injuries reported.**
* **Product and packaging damage** from pallet collapse.

Recommendations

*Suspend and revoke the associate’s PIT license pending review.
*Require mandatory comprehensive retrai

On 8/12/2022 at approximately 7:41pm, a process assistant (PA) was unloading a pallet out of dock door 170 when the top pallet they were attempting to down stack caused both of the stacked pallets to fall onto the ground. Upon investigating, it was determined that the AA was not at fault. The top pallet was discovered to contain more cases than the pallet on the bottom. Not only were there more cases, but there was a weight difference between the cases inside the top pallet and the cases inside the bottom pallet. The top pallet contained several heavy cases of protein shakes, while the bottom contained cases that were large in length but light in weight.  The process assistant did not have the ability to see the weight nor case difference due to the two pallets being Universal Plastic Pallets (UPP) and being covered by side panels. A heavy pallet should always be stacked on the bottom to have more stability. In the footage, the two side panels of the bottom pallet began to bulge out. Due to the thin poly sheet composite of the side panels of the UPP pallets, such bulging occurs frequently when the forks enter the pallet but then readjust after the top pallet gets down stacked. The PA believed the bulging would readjust since it typically does, but due to the heavy weight of the top pallet plus the added weight of the forks from PIT RC #1, such bottom pallet bulged out excessively and lost its stability causing both pallets to tumble down. The PA is not at fault, heavy pallets should be stacked at the bottom to maintain stability something the site where the pallets were stacked did not ensure.

Date of Incident: 9/24/2025
Time: 10:50 AM
Location: Pit Lane by Pick Desk
Equipment: Order Picker
Incident Type: Near Miss - Equipment Contact
Training date: 5/12/2025

Incident Description:
At 10:50 AM, a near miss incident occurred when an Order Picker operator attempted to maneuver in a congested pit lane area near the Pick desk. The operator on OP 136 was initially traveling against the designated direction of travel when they stopped upon realizing their error. Instead of proceeding to the designated turn-around point, the operator attempted to back up between two stationary OPs that were waiting in line for cage exchange. The spacing between the stationary OPs was insufficient for this maneuver, and during the backward movement, the front of the operator's OP contacted the forks of a stationary OP 56. At the time of the incident, the pit lane was experiencing increased congestion due to multiple OPs queuing for cage exchanges, with equipment positioned closer than the required blue light safety distance of 8 feet. As immediate corrective action, the associate will be retrained on proper PIT operation procedures, traffic patterns, and safety protocols.

Witness Statement:

On 2/20/2025 two RME technicians were working on a segmented belt leading into the divert 8 spiral off the outbound/shipping sorter. The technicians were doing a standard belt replacement and got permission from Operations to make the repair from 06:25-07:05. It was observed by another technician that was working next to them that the two technicians working on the segment belt had not locked out the spiral. While the technicians were not working on the spiral itself, it is required to lock out the spiral per the 6-foot rule. The observing technician then used his stop work authority and notified the other two technicians of the miss. This incident is a LOTO Violation.

During the investigation it was discovered that when the stop the job was issued, 1 technician went down and locked out the equipment while the other stayed and continued working on the segmented belt. Both technicians should have stopped immediately and locked out the spiral together. Management was notified of the issue shortly thereafter. The technicians in question took responsibility for their miss and provided witness statements to their AMM, and an incident report was submitted with all the details. RMM’s on both the JLL and Amazon side were notified, as well as Regional EHS and site safety. Photos of the incident area were provided to all parties. The technician who remained at the spiral indicated in their witness statement that they were complacent in acknowledging the 6 foot rule.
